discipline_framing: Political science, social-movement theory, policy analysis, and environmental studies applied to how elections, regulation, geopolitics, movements, and climate shape consumer trends
audience: Trend analysts, strategists, risk and public-affairs teams, and researchers who must anticipate how political events, regulation, social movements, and environmental change redirect consumer and market trends
sources: The PESTEL/STEEP macro-environment scanning tradition in strategic management
Tarrow, Power in Movement, and Tilly's work on social movements — political-process and mobilization theory
Benford & Snow on collective-action framing; Hirschman, Exit, Voice, and Loyalty for consumer-political action
Boycott and political-consumerism research (Glickman, Edited Volume 'Boycotts'; Micheletti's political virtualism; Neilson's data on boycott/buycott prevalence)
IPCC assessment reports and climate-communication research for environmental drivers
Regulatory-impact and policy-cycle literature (Kingdon's multiple-streams model of agenda and windows)
Scenario-planning practice (Shell lineage, Schwartz's Art of the Long View) for macro-uncertainty handling
pitfalls: Headline-reactive analysis — treating every political event as a trend driver without assessing magnitude, duration, and transmission channels
Assuming stated values equal behavior — the documented attitude-action gap in ethical and political consumption
Ignoring policy lags — regulation proposed, passed, enforced, and felt on very different timelines
Single-country framing of global drivers — elections, wars, and climate effects transmit across borders unevenly
Scenario planning without probabilities, triggers, or monitoring — scenarios as decoration rather than decision tools
